extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of comedy, literary critics, playwrights, and philosophers of humor
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative criteria and production techniques from Bergson's Laughter: essay on what makes things comic (mechanisation vs life; devices such as repetition, inversion, and interference). Useful for analysing or composing comic situations, lines, and stagecraft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person-as-thing / mechanization of the human
rubrics_metrics.description: "WE LAUGH EVERY TIME A PERSON GIVES US THE IMPRESSION OF BEING A THING."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core principle: comic effect arises when a human appears to lose living suppleness and to behave like an object or machine. Examples: clowns whose movements suggest rubber balls or wooden dummies; Sancho Panza tumbled like a football; Baron Munchausen as a cannon-ball. Guidance: emphasise rigidity, automatism, or the viewer's shift from seeing a person to seeing a thing; build the impression gradually (see gradual suggestion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradual suggestion (vague-to-clear transformation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a progressively clarified image: start from an indefinite perception and make it more distinct so the audience accepts the suggested transformation (analogy to hypnotic suggestion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: introduce blurred or vague traits, then accentuate them step by step until the audience's imagination completes the transformation (e.g., gestures becoming rounder until bodies appear like balls). Poets achieve similar effects by rhythm, rhyme, and assonance that lull the imagination. Examples: hypnotic suggestion, falling-off-to-sleep imagery, Regnard and Figaro lines that arouse the fleeting image of a doll or animal. Practical note: gradualness makes extraordinary identifications believable and thus laughable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talking about persons as things / confusing person with function
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic arises when people are referred to or treated as impersonal objects or functions rather than as persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: M. Perrichon listing parcels with his wife/daughter as items; saying kings 'that have occurred' likening them to impersonal events; confusing a person with his office ('the prefect... has been changed several times'). Use feigned confusion between person and function to create an impersonal, mechanical tone that elicits laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the joke 'acceptable' by fitting state of mind or circumstance
rubrics_metrics.description: A witticism is accepted (and thus effective) when it seems the natural product of a character's state of mind or fits the surrounding circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The skill is not merely inventing a joke but giving it suggestive power so the audience accepts the identification—use character psychology, repeated lessons or phrases, or situational credibility (e.g., Perrichon's excitation on first journey makes his parcel-counting plausible). If the joke feels forced or out-of-character, it will fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composite definition of a comic situation
rubrics_metrics.description: "ANY ARRANGEMENT OF ACTS AND EVENTS IS COMIC WHICH GIVES US, IN A SINGLE COMBINATION, THE ILLUSION OF LIFE AND THE DISTINCT IMPRESSION OF A MECHANICAL ARRANGEMENT."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A comic situation must simultaneously suggest living animation and the presence of a mechanical contrivance beneath it. When both impressions coexist, the contrast generates laughter. Use this as a litmus test when constructing scenes: do they retain some life yet reveal an underlying automatism?

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition (general device)
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition of words or situations produces comic effect by symbolising a mechanical, spring-like play of opposing forces (life vs mechanism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two scales: (a) verbal repetition on stage signals a repressed feeling repeatedly sprung and repressed (see 'word-repetition' entry); (b) situational repetition—the same scene or incident reproduced several times—creates a sense of mechanical recurrence. Effective repetition is made funnier the more complex and naturally introduced the repeated scene is (e.g., Molière's use of three tempi). Repetition can occur across acts or with different character groups (masters vs servants).

rubrics_metrics.name: Word-repetition: two-term model (spring and repression)
rubrics_metrics.description: In comic word-repetition we generally find two terms: a repressed feeling which 'goes off like a spring', and an idea that delights in repressing the feeling anew.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Dorine's storytelling where 'Et Tartuffe?' keeps recurring; Scapin playing with Geronte's avarice; Harpagon's recurring 'No dowry wanted!' Use repetition to symbolise an automatic internal conflict (e.g., a man oscillating between blunt honesty and learned politeness). The voice, tempo, and increasing forcefulness of repetition should signal the mounting internal tension until a comic release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jack-in-the-box image (spring/tempo/staccato rhythm)
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic pattern modelled on the jack-in-the-box: a force repeatedly bent and released, producing a rhythmic up-and-down tempo that is laughable because it makes living beings resemble a mechanical toy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage technique: rhythm and tempo (regular beats, recurring entrances/exits) emphasise mechanical automatism. Examples: Punch and Judy policeman flopping and springing back; scenes where characters re-enter repeatedly at regular intervals (Purgon/Argan TEMPO). Use physical rhythm or verbal beats to create the 'spring' sensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dancing-jack / puppetry (manipulation by another)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy occurs when a character seems to act freely but is perceived as a puppet controlled by another agent or by external strings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: make one character evidently pulling strings (manipulator) while another behaves like a puppet; personify opposing choices or decisions so they appear as separate actors on the puppet-strings. Examples: Scapin manipulating Geronte and Argante; Panurge vacillating with personified options. Dramatic effect: audience may side with the manipulator or enjoy the spectacle of another's agency being denied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Snow-ball / cumulative escalation (arithmetical progression)
rubrics_metrics.description: A small cause produces successively larger effects (a rolling snow-ball), so that insignificant beginnings culminate in an unexpectedly large or disastrous outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use chain reactions or concatenations of incidents that accelerate or multiply consequences (toy soldiers, house of cards, chain of mishaps in picture-stories). Examples: the mule-driver → Sancho → Maritornes → innkeeper chain; Labiche's hat that keeps slipping away and escalating complications; lawsuits within lawsuits. This device can be linear or circular (see reversibility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversibility / circular return
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanisms that are reversible or circular—efforts that ultimately bring one back to the starting point—heighten comic effect by turning exertion into null result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Children enjoy seeing a mechanism undo itself; comedies exploit the delight in return-to-origin (e.g., journeys ending where they began, quests that retrieve what was already lost). Although 'effort meeting a void' (Spencer/Kant) can illustrate this, Bergson warns lack-of-proportion alone is insufficient; the laughable element is the revealed mechanical arrangement and the 'absentmindedness' in life that allowed it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection of mechanical arrangement as absentmindedness
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic points out an 'absentmindedness' in life — moments when actions or events betray inattention, automatism, or inelasticity — and laughter functions as a social corrective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct scenes that reveal how human continuity has been interrupted by rigid, mechanical sequences (coincidences, automatism). Bergson treats laughter as a gesture that singles out and represses this social imperfection; in performance, invite audience recognition of the absentminded mechanism to produce shared corrective laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three abstract methods: repetition, inversion, reciprocal interference
rubrics_metrics.description: Bergson's taxonomy: the counterparts of life (continuity, irreversibility, individuality) give rise to three comic processes — REPETITION, INVERSION, and RECIPROCAL INTERFERENCE OF SERIES.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a high-level framework when analysing or composing comedy: (a) repetition — recurrence of words/situations; (b) inversion — reversal of expected temporal or logical order (introduced here as an essential method though elaboration appears later in the essay); (c) reciprocal interference of series — crossing or collision of otherwise independent series of events producing mechanical outcomes. Each of these can be instantiated by devices described elsewhere (jack-in-the-box, snow-ball, dancing-jack).
